title: From House Records to a Price Guess
key_insight: When tomorrow's house has features but no known price, scikit-learn offers one dependable route: create a model, fit past examples, then predict the unseen case.
body:
## A Price for Tomorrow's House

Past houses have sizes, ages, and known prices; tomorrow's house has no price yet. First choose a model and create one copy of it.

Fit means show that model the past inputs and their known answers so it can learn a pattern. Predict means give it new inputs and ask it to use that pattern.

Keep some answered houses out of fitting. Testing on those untouched rows shows whether the model learned a useful rule instead of merely remembering its homework.
common_mistakes: Calling `predict` before `fit` — the model has not learned any relationship yet.
Fitting on the test data — that turns the supposed check into more training data.
Mixing up `X` and `y` — `X` holds input features; `y` holds the answers or targets.
Changing the split on every run and then comparing scores as if the data stayed identical.
mini_exercise: Write the four core lines—import, create, fit, predict—on separate cards and arrange them. Then explain what information is available at each step.
real_world_usage: Analysts use this same fit/predict pattern for price forecasting, churn prediction, fraud screening, and many other classical machine-learning tasks.
explain_back_prompt: Tell the house-price story from raw rows to unseen predictions. Why must the test rows stay out of `fit`?
